title: europes deepening drought 2026 08 11
text:
Hello!
Water shortages and drought have hit nations in Europe and Africa as temperatures continue to swelter around the world.
An estimated 204 million people, 56% of Western Europe's population, are forecast to experience temperatures over 5 degrees Celsius (10 degrees Fahrenheit) or more above the historic norm for this time of year on Tuesday, according to Reuters Climate Monitor.
Our Reuters photographers have also captured some eye-catching images around Europe as historic drought conditions on the continent throw up another ​side effect: revealing medieval buildings, ancient bridges and Nazi shipwrecks.Click here
, opens new tab
 to see more.
Italy's Po River Basin Authority has issued a high-severity drought warning as water levels in Alpine lakes fall, while Britain said more than 70% of ‌the country is experiencing flash drought conditions after months of low rainfall and unusually high temperatures.
Over in South Africa, water shortages have become a symbol of municipal failures that have angered voters and eroded support for the ruling African National Congress, as the nation prepares for local elections expected by November.
* Europe’s record heat and droughts
Record heat and droughts this summer – which scientists say are exacerbated by global warming – have wreaked havoc in power production, shipping and public health systems, while this wildfire season is on track to be Europe's biggest ever.
Climate is changing more rapidly in Europe than on any other continent and the damage is already stretching public finances, ​setting off wild swings in inflation, redrawing the tourism map, and forcing the bloc to rethink how power is produced and how goods are transported.
Traffic on the Rhine and the Danube rivers, key cargo arteries, is severely limited because of low ​water levels, more than a half dozen nuclear generators have shut or curtailed production due to cooling difficulties.
Agricultural yield estimates have been cut with crops harvested late, such as maize and sunflower, suffering a ⁠6-7% loss already in July.
Italy is Europe's largest rice producer, with about 235,000 hectares planted in 2025, according to the national rice authority. More than 80% of the crop is grown in the northern provinces which have long thrived on the Po basin, but this year, ​the local authorities have issued a high level of drought severity.
Lake Maggiore is now classified as being in extreme drought conditions, while water levels in the Po recently fell to a record low for the time of year in Cremona.
In England, roughly 45 million people are in a drought ​area and 27 million are living under restrictions on water use, according to Britain’s government. Rivers, reservoirs, and groundwater levels continue to decline while the continued hot and dry conditions are increasing the risk of wildfires, the government said.
* ‘Maintenance is not sexy’
In South Africa, Johannesburg Water, the utility owned and run by the local authority, acknowledges there is a problem with its water maintenance.
"Maintenance is not sexy. It's always more interesting to allocate funds to other areas," Craig Sheridan, director and founder of the Centre in Water Research and Development at the city's University of the Witwatersrand, told Reuters.
Analysts say climate change is worsening the city's water ​woes by increasing the amount lost to evaporation.
Another underlying problem is the mounting budgetary crisis at the City of Johannesburg Metropolitan Municipality.
"The infrastructure is old. A lot of it is more than 50 years old," its senior manager for innovation and technology, Zakhele Khuzwayo, told Reuters ​in an interview.
"The city is aware of the limitations. We know where we'd like to be ... Now it's a matter of paving the way to get there."

* Talking Points
* In Conversation
Dr. Naveen Rao, senior vice president of the health initiative at the Rockefeller Foundation, shares his thoughts on rising temperatures and public health:
“As devastating wildfires and unprecedented heat drive crises around the world, we must stop treating extreme heat as simply a weather event.
“It is a pressing public health emergency. Heat is already claiming lives, making people sick, and disrupting education and livelihoods, imposing enormous economic costs, especially on the world’s most vulnerable populations.
“Yet, just as these risks are accelerating, shrinking development assistance for ⁠health and rising debt ​are making it harder for many countries to prepare. Waiting for the next crisis is no longer an option.
“We know what works. The challenge now is to ​bring together science and technology, locally led action, and innovative financing to build resilient health systems that protect communities before the next heat emergency strikes.”
* ESG Spotlight
Sharks – can’t live with them, but apparently we can get some insights on hurricanes, according to scientists in the University of Delaware.
Click here for an insightful story on how these scary sea ​predators are helping researchers understand more about hurricanes, as they can serve as mobile near-real-time ocean-data observers, carrying sensors that measure ocean conditions to inform oceanographic, atmospheric and climate models.
